abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a revolutionary paradigm for understanding and designing self-organizing mechanisms in mobile ad hoc networks by leveraging complex adaptive systems theory. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on deterministic routing tables and centralized control, we propose modeling network topology evolution as an emergent phenomenon arising from local interactions among nodes. Our theoretical framework establishes that the dynamics of network self-organization can be accurately characterized through coupled differential equations describing information propagation, energy consumption, and mobility patterns. We prove mathematically that under mild conditions, globally coherent network structures emerge from purely local decision-making rules, eliminating the need for explicit coordination protocols. The framework fundamentally reframes medium access control as a synchronization problem in dynamical systems rather than a scheduling optimization task. Simulation results across diverse mobility models demonstrate that networks following our emergent paradigm achieve 40% higher packet delivery ratios while consuming 35% less energy compared to state-of-the-art protocols. This work opens entirely new research directions by establishing theoretical foundations for organic network evolution, shifting the paradigm from engineered protocols to designed interaction rules that give rise to desired network behaviors.

This paper presents a rigorous analytical framework for performance evaluation and optimization of geographic routing protocols in vehicular ad hoc networks under realistic urban conditions. We develop a novel queueing-theoretic model that accurately captures the complex interplay between vehicle mobility patterns, road topology, and communication channel characteristics. The proposed model incorporates spatial queuing theory to characterize multi-hop packet delivery in sparse and dense traffic scenarios, addressing the fundamental limitation of existing analyses that assume homogeneous node distribution. Through extensive Markov chain analysis, we derive closed-form expressions for key performance metrics including end-to-end delay, packet delivery ratio, and hop count distribution. Our analysis reveals that optimal transmission range exhibits a non-linear relationship with vehicle density, contradicting widely adopted assumptions in protocol design. Based on these theoretical insights, we formulate an adaptive transmission power control strategy that maximizes network throughput while maintaining energy efficiency. Numerical results demonstrate that protocols designed according to our analytical framework achieve up to 28% improvement in packet delivery ratio and 45% reduction in control overhead compared to conventional geographic routing approaches. The theoretical contributions provide design guidelines for next-generation vehicular network protocols.

We introduce CrossChain, a groundbreaking network architecture that fundamentally transforms data forwarding in opportunistic networks through blockchain-inspired consensus mechanisms. Unlike conventional store-carry-forward approaches that suffer from arbitrary relay selection and unpredictable delivery delays, CrossChain establishes a decentralized reputation system where nodes collectively determine forwarding decisions through a novel proof-of-cooperation consensus protocol. The system architecture comprises three integrated components: a distributed ledger maintaining forwarding history, a smart contract layer enforcing cooperation incentives, and a dynamic routing engine adapting to network conditions. Each node maintains locally computed reputation scores while global consensus is achieved through lightweight cryptographic verification, eliminating single points of failure inherent in centralized approaches. CrossChain introduces a paradigm shift by transforming selfish node behavior from a threat into a network optimization opportunity, as nodes are economically motivated to make globally optimal forwarding decisions. We implement a fully functional prototype on commodity hardware and evaluate performance through trace-driven simulations using real mobility data from urban environments. Results demonstrate that CrossChain achieves 52% higher delivery ratios and 60% lower average delays compared to existing epidemic and spray-and-wait protocols, while maintaining robust security against Sybil and false-reporting attacks. This architecture establishes a new design paradigm for delay-tolerant networks.

This paper presents EnergyStar, a comprehensive energy-efficient MAC protocol designed for battery-constrained mobile ad hoc networks that significantly advances the state of the art in duty-cycling mechanisms. The proposed protocol introduces a novel adaptive synchronization framework that dynamically adjusts listen and sleep periods based on real-time traffic prediction and node mobility patterns. Energystar incorporates three key innovations: a traffic-aware slot allocation algorithm that reduces idle listening by 70%, a mobility-adaptive synchronization mechanism that maintains network connectivity with 40% fewer synchronization packets, and an interference-aware channel selection scheme that improves spatial reuse without increasing collision probability. The protocol architecture leverages cross-layer information from both network and application layers to make intelligent power management decisions, representing a significant departure from traditional MAC-layer-only approaches. We implement Energystar on IEEE 802.11 hardware and conduct extensive experiments in indoor and outdoor testbeds with varying node densities. Experimental results demonstrate that Energystar extends network lifetime by 180% compared to standard 802.11 PSM while maintaining comparable throughput and latency performance. The protocol also shows superior performance under dynamic traffic conditions, with less than 5% degradation in energy efficiency when traffic patterns change abruptly. Energystar provides a practical, deployable solution for energy-constrained ad hoc and sensor networks.
